title: Plant Growth and Development
description: Grade 11 Biology: phases of plant growth and differentiation, the five plant growth regulators (auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene, ABA), and photoperiodism and vernalisation.

topics.title: Growth, Differentiation and Development
topics.concept:
Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in the size of a part or the whole organism, usually accompanied by an increase in dry weight. In plants, growth is special because it continues throughout life — this is called indeterminate growth — thanks to special regions of dividing cells called meristems at the root and shoot tips and in the thickening tissues.

Growth at the cell level happens in three phases: the phase of cell division (in the meristem), the phase of cell enlargement (cells grow larger and take up water in a vacuole), and the phase of cell maturation (cells take their final shape and function). If you plot size against time, growth typically follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve — slow at first, then rapid, then slowing as it levels off.

Cells then become specialised for particular jobs — this is differentiation (for example, a simple cell becoming a water-carrying xylem vessel). Two related terms are dedifferentiation (a mature cell regaining the ability to divide, e.g. forming cork cambium) and redifferentiation (those cells maturing again into a new tissue). The whole sequence of growth, differentiation and maturation that leads to the adult plant is called development. Plants also show plasticity — they can change their form in response to the environment (for example, growing different-shaped leaves in water and in air).

examples.problem: Example 1: What is growth, and where does it mainly occur in plants?
examples.solution:
Recall the definition and the special tissue.

  • Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size (and dry weight).
  • It mainly occurs at the meristems (root and shoot tips).
examples.answer: Growth is an irreversible increase in size; in plants it occurs mainly at the meristems.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the three phases of growth at the cell level.
examples.solution:
Cells go through three stages.

  • Cell division, cell enlargement, and cell maturation.
examples.answer: Cell division, cell enlargement (elongation), and cell maturation.

examples.solution:
Cells take on special roles.

  • Differentiation is the process by which cells become specialised for particular functions.
examples.answer: Differentiation is the process by which cells become structurally and functionally specialised.

recap:
• Growth = irreversible increase in size; plants grow throughout life (meristems; indeterminate growth).
  • Three phases: division → enlargement → maturation; growth follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.
  • Differentiation (specialisation); dedifferentiation & redifferentiation.
  • Development = whole sequence to adult; plants show plasticity.

quiz.q: Growth in plants mainly occurs at regions of dividing cells called:
quiz.explanation: Meristems are the regions of active cell division responsible for growth.

quiz.q: A typical growth curve plotted over time is:
quiz.explanation: Plant growth typically follows a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.

topics.title: Plant Growth Regulators (Hormones)
topics.concept:
Plants control their growth and development using chemical messengers called plant growth regulators (PGRs) or plant hormones — substances made in one part of the plant and active in tiny amounts. There are five main groups, broadly divided into growth promoters and growth inhibitors.

  • Auxins — promote cell elongation; control phototropism and geotropism (bending toward light and gravity), promote rooting in cuttings, and cause apical dominance (the main shoot tip suppresses side branches). Used to prevent fruit drop and as weedkillers.
  • Gibberellins (GA) — promote stem elongation (can make dwarf plants tall), help seeds germinate by breaking dormancy, and promote bolting and flowering.
  • Cytokinins — promote cell division, help form new shoots/buds, and delay ageing of leaves (delay senescence).
  • Ethylene — a gaseous hormone; ripens fruits, promotes ageing and falling of leaves and fruits (abscission), and breaks dormancy.
  • Abscisic acid (ABA) — the main growth inhibitor; called the "stress hormone" because it closes stomata during water shortage, promotes dormancy of seeds and buds, and counters the growth promoters.

In real plants, growth is decided not by one hormone alone but by the balance between promoters and inhibitors. Farmers and gardeners use PGRs to root cuttings, ripen fruit, increase yield, and control weeds.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which hormone is responsible for apical dominance?
examples.solution:
The shoot tip suppresses side branches.

  • Auxin, made at the shoot tip, causes apical dominance.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the gaseous plant hormone and one of its effects.
examples.solution:
One hormone is a gas.

  • Ethylene is the gaseous hormone.
  • It ripens fruits (and promotes abscission of leaves/fruits).
examples.answer: Ethylene; it ripens fruits (and promotes leaf/fruit fall).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is abscisic acid called the stress hormone?
examples.solution:
It helps the plant cope with stress.

  • ABA closes stomata during water shortage to reduce water loss.
  • It also promotes dormancy, helping the plant survive bad conditions.
examples.answer: Because ABA closes stomata in water stress and promotes dormancy, helping the plant survive harsh conditions.

recap:
• 5 PGRs: promoters = auxin (elongation, tropisms, apical dominance, rooting), gibberellin (stem elongation, germination), cytokinin (cell division, delays senescence); also ethylene (gas; ripening, abscission).
  • Inhibitor = abscisic acid (ABA) — "stress hormone", closes stomata, dormancy.
  • Growth depends on the balance of promoters and inhibitors.

quiz.q: The hormone mainly responsible for fruit ripening is:
quiz.explanation: Ethylene, a gaseous hormone, ripens fruits.

quiz.q: The 'stress hormone' that closes stomata and promotes dormancy is:
quiz.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the stress hormone and a growth inhibitor.

topics.title: Photoperiodism and Vernalisation
topics.concept:
Plants do not flower at just any time — many time their flowering to the length of day and night, or to a spell of cold. These responses help a plant flower in the right season.

Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night (the photoperiod). Based on their flowering needs, plants are grouped as:

  • Long-day plants — flower when the day is longer than a critical length (e.g. wheat, spinach).
  • Short-day plants — flower when the day is shorter than a critical length (e.g. rice, chrysanthemum).
  • Day-neutral plants — flowering does not depend on day length (e.g. tomato, cucumber).

The day length is sensed by the leaves (through a pigment), which then send a signal (a hormone, sometimes called florigen) to the shoot tips to make them flower.

Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature (cold treatment). Some plants, especially certain winter varieties of wheat and other crops, will not flower unless they first experience a cold spell. This makes sure they flower at the proper time after winter, and not too early. Both photoperiodism and vernalisation are examples of how plants "read" their environment to develop at the right time.

examples.solution:
It is a response to day length.

  • Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night, affecting flowering.
examples.answer: Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the relative lengths of day and night (the photoperiod), especially for flowering.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which part of the plant senses the day length?
examples.solution:
One organ perceives the photoperiod.

  • The leaves sense the day length and send a signal to the shoot tips.
examples.answer: The leaves sense the day length (and signal the shoot tips to flower).

examples.solution:
It involves cold.

  • Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature (cold treatment).
examples.answer: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by exposure to a period of low temperature (cold).

recap:
• Photoperiodism: flowering response to day/night length. Long-day (wheat), short-day (rice, chrysanthemum), day-neutral (tomato).
  • Leaves sense the photoperiod and signal the shoot tips (florigen).
  • Vernalisation: cold treatment that promotes flowering (e.g. winter wheat).
  • Both let plants flower at the right season.

quiz.q: Flowering response to the relative length of day and night is called:
quiz.explanation: Photoperiodism is the response to day/night length.

quiz.q: Promotion of flowering by a cold treatment is called:
quiz.explanation: Vernalisation is the cold treatment that promotes flowering.

questions.q: Growth is best defined as a/an:
questions.explanation: Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size.

questions.q: Plant growth continues through life because of regions called:
questions.explanation: Meristems provide indeterminate growth throughout life.

questions.q: The three phases of growth at the cell level are division, enlargement and:
questions.explanation: The phases are division, enlargement and maturation.

questions.q: A typical growth curve is:
questions.explanation: Plant growth follows a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.

questions.q: The process by which cells become specialised is:
questions.explanation: Differentiation is the specialisation of cells.

questions.q: The hormone that promotes cell elongation and apical dominance is:
questions.explanation: Auxin promotes elongation and causes apical dominance.

questions.q: Which hormone helps dwarf plants grow tall and breaks seed dormancy?
questions.explanation: Gibberellins promote stem elongation and germination.

questions.q: Cytokinins mainly promote:
questions.explanation: Cytokinins promote cell division and delay senescence.

questions.q: The gaseous plant hormone is:
questions.explanation: Ethylene is the gaseous hormone that ripens fruit.

questions.q: The main growth inhibitor and 'stress hormone' is:
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the stress hormone and inhibitor.

questions.q: Apical dominance means the shoot tip:
options: Suppresses the growth of side branches
questions.explanation: Auxin from the tip suppresses lateral buds — apical dominance.

questions.q: Response of plants to the length of day and night is:
questions.explanation: Photoperiodism is the response to photoperiod.

questions.q: Plants that flower only when days are shorter than a critical length are:
questions.explanation: Short-day plants (e.g. rice) flower with short days.

questions.q: The plant part that senses day length is the:
questions.explanation: Leaves perceive the photoperiod and signal the shoot tips.

questions.q: Promotion of flowering by exposure to cold is:
questions.explanation: Vernalisation is the cold treatment that promotes flowering.

questions.q: Removing the shoot tip of a plant makes the side branches grow more. This is because the tip normally supplies:
questions.explanation: The tip's auxin suppresses lateral buds; removing it releases the side branches to grow.

questions.q: Storing unripe bananas with a ripe apple speeds up their ripening because the apple releases:
questions.explanation: Ripe fruit releases ethylene, a gaseous hormone that triggers ripening in nearby fruit.

questions.q: During a drought, a plant's stomata close mainly due to a rise in:
questions.explanation: ABA, the stress hormone, accumulates in water stress and closes stomata to conserve water.

questions.q: A short-day plant kept under long days will most likely:
questions.explanation: Short-day plants need short days (long nights) to flower; long days prevent flowering.

questions.q: Winter wheat sown in spring without a cold spell does not flower well. This shows the need for:
questions.explanation: Such varieties require a cold period (vernalisation) before they can flower.

questions.q: The fact that a single plant can grow differently shaped leaves underwater and in air illustrates:
questions.explanation: Changing form in response to the environment is plasticity (heterophylly is one example).
